1.pericope_label: And it came to pass in the four hundred and eightieth year after the children of Israel were come out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel, in the month Zif, which is the second month, that he began to build the house of the Lord. And the house which king Solomon built for the Lord, the length thereof was threescore cubits, and the breadth thereof twenty cubits, and the height thereof thirty cubits. And the porch before the temple of the house, twenty cubits was the length thereof, according to the breadth of the house; and ten cubits was the breadth thereof before the house. And for the house he made windows of narrow lights. And against the wall of the house he built chambers round about, against the walls of the house round about, both of the temple and of the oracle: and he made chambers round about: The nethermost chamber was five cubits broad, and the middle was six cubits broad, and the third was seven cubits broad: for without in the wall of the house he made narrowed rests round about, that the beams should not be fastened in the walls of the house. And the house, when it was in building, was built of stone made ready before it was brought thither: so that there was neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron heard in the house, while it was in building. The door for the middle chamber was in the right side of the house: and they went up with winding stairs into the middle chamber, and out of the middle into the third. So he built the house, and finished it; and covered the house with beams and boards of cedar. And then he built chambers against all the house, five cubits high: and they rested on the house with timber of cedar.

schools.summary: Ellicott defends the date of the fourth year against the charge of interpolation, explaining the Septuagint's 440 as an interchange of two similar Hebrew letters and Josephus's 592 as a possible tacit harmony with some reckoning known among the heathen, and arguing that a date disagreeing at first sight with the earlier indications is the last thing a scribe would have inserted. He also sees that the temple copies the tabernacle with each dimension doubled, so that it is eight times the cubical contents and still a small building, not larger than a good-sized parish church and in plan oddly like a Gothic one, a resemblance he lays to the old Freemasonry which took Solomon's plan for a sacred guide. On the windows he grants the splayed reading good authorities but prefers fixed lattices, and on the silent building he calls the provision one of reverence, suspecting that the prohibition of tools on the altar suggested it. Delitzsch gives the Mosaic cubit in Parisian lines, rejects the hundred and twenty cubits assigned the porch in Chronicles against Ewald and Stieglitz, denies that the windows were broad within and narrow without in favour of windows with closed beams, settles that the stones were not unhewn but perfectly tooled in the quarry, and describes the side building in detail, its three stories widening from five cubits to seven on rebates cut in the temple wall so that nothing was inserted into the wall itself.

Gill reckons the four hundred and eighty years rather than arguing them, and offers two different tallies of the intervening periods. On the side chambers he observes that they stood against the two long sides and the west end only, since the porch occupied the east, and that the beams were not fastened into the wall; and he reckons the upper chambers separately, suggesting that the disciples after the ascension may have been in one of them.

Clarke assembles more than a dozen chronologists on the date, from Glycas at 330 years to Serarius at 680, and concludes that the figure in the common Hebrew text is as likely to be the true one as any of them. He converts the cubits to yards, feet and inches on Cumberland's figure and then declines to describe the building at all, since men professing the same principles have produced very different ones, deferring to the description he prints at the end of the chapter. He takes the windows for lattices open within and shut without, notes that we hear nothing of glass or any other diaphanous substance, and hazards that window was once windore, a door to let the wind in; on the silence he asks why the point is so particularly marked and answers that the temple was a type, the stones squared and fitted here for their place in the New Jerusalem. On the roofing he observes that Eastern practice is the reverse of ours, plaster floors and wooden ceilings.

Henry reckons the years with Gill and then turns to the lessons. The doubled dimensions are provision for a people grown both more numerous and richer. The windows broad within and narrow without teach that our minds should look much within to judge ourselves and little without to censure our brethren, their narrowness also intimating the darkness of that dispensation. The stones prepared beforehand are first a rule of prudence and then a lesson, that quietness and silence both become and befriend religious exercises and that God's work should be done with as much care and as little noise as may be, against which he sets the psalm where the destroyers roared in the congregation: clamour and violence often hinder the work of God but never further it. The side chambers were vestries for the utensils and for the priests to dress in, and the care taken not to fasten the beams into the wall warns that the church's strength should not be impaired under pretence of adding to its beauty.

debates.question: How is the four hundred and eightieth year to be treated?

positions.position: Defended as genuine and formally given, the Septuagint and Josephus both explicable and neither outweighing the present text
Left open among more than a dozen conflicting reckonings, with the common Hebrew text as likely as any
Simply added up from the wilderness, Joshua, the judges, Eli, Samuel and Saul, David and Solomon

debates.question: What are the windows of narrow lights?

Latticed, open within and shut without, so that one inside could see well and one outside nothing
Windows with closed beams, fixed lattices that could not be opened at pleasure, the received gloss agreeing with the fact but not the words
Fixed lattices, immovable so that none could look out or in, the splayed reading granted good authorities but not preferred

Out of reverence, possibly suggested by the prohibition of tools on the altar, though the idea there was different
Because the stones were so perfectly tooled when broken in the quarry that no iron was required at the building

11.pericope_label: And the word of the Lord came to Solomon, saying, Concerning this house which thou art in building, if thou wilt walk in my statutes, and execute my judgments, and keep all my commandments to walk in them; then will I perform my word with thee, which I spake unto David thy father: And I will dwell among the children of Israel, and will not forsake my people Israel. So Solomon built the house, and finished it.

schools.summary: Delitzsch reasons about the medium from the phrasing, that the word of the Lord came seems to point to a prophet, which agrees with the later notice that God revealed himself to Solomon by an actual appearance only twice. On the construction he is alone: the house stands at the head absolutely, so the sense runs as for the house which thou art building, if thou walkest in my statutes, then I will set up my word; and the word meant is the promise of an everlasting throne made to David. On that reading the assurance that God will dwell among the children of Israel adds no second promise but applies the old one to the building now begun.

Gill calls it a word of prophecy with the Targum and allows either an impulse of the Spirit or the hand of a prophet, noting that Kimchi prefers the second and that some Jewish writers name Ahijah the Shilonite. Following Abarbinel he explains the timing, that the message came in the midst of the work to keep Solomon from depending on the strength of the fabric, since its perpetuity hung on his own conduct and his successors' and the people's; conscious of his integrity and hoping well of posterity, Solomon was not discouraged but carried the work to perfection, encouraged by the promise of the divine presence provided a proper regard was had to the will and ways of God.

Clarke takes up the question of identity, whether this is the same revelation as the one recorded after the dedication. Some think it is; to him it appears different, a word given while the building was going forward, to encourage Solomon, to warn him against apostasy, and to assure him of continued protection if he and his family remained faithful to the grace given them.

Henry gives the fullest account of why the message came in the middle of the work, in two parts. First for encouragement, since the great care, expense and fatigue might well have made Solomon wish he had never begun, and an eye to the promise will carry a man cheerfully through his work. Second for admonition, the condition annexed being there to make him consider that he might build the temple ever so strong and its glory would still depart unless he and his people continued to walk in God's statutes, since all that charge would neither excuse them from obedience to the law nor shelter them from judgment in case of disobedience. From this he draws the sharpest sentence in the chapter, that keeping God's commandments is better and more pleasing to him than building churches, and adds that none employ themselves for God without having his eye upon them, and that the strictness of God's government will never drive a good man from his service but quicken him in it.

debates.question: By what means did the word reach Solomon?

positions.position: By a prophetic medium, since God appeared to Solomon in person only twice
By an impulse of the Spirit or by a prophet, whom some Jewish writers name as Ahijah the Shilonite
Not the same revelation as the one after the dedication, but a distinct word given while the building went forward

debates.question: Why was the promise given while the work was still in hand?

positions.position: For encouragement in a wearying work and for admonition that the building excuses nothing
To keep Solomon from depending on the strength of the fabric, its perpetuity hanging on conduct
To encourage, to warn against apostasy, and to assure of continued protection if they remained faithful

positions.position: No, only a special application of the promise made to David of an everlasting throne
A widening of the loving-kindness, to Solomon in the performing of the word and to his kingdom in the dwelling

15.pericope_label: And he built the walls of the house within with boards of cedar, both the floor of the house, and the walls of the cieling: and he covered them on the inside with wood, and covered the floor of the house with planks of fir. And he built twenty cubits on the sides of the house, both the floor and the walls with boards of cedar: he even built them for it within, even for the oracle, even for the most holy place. And the house, that is, the temple before it, was forty cubits long. And the cedar of the house within was carved with knops and open flowers: all was cedar; there was no stone seen. And the oracle he prepared in the house within, to set there the ark of the covenant of the Lord. And the oracle in the forepart was twenty cubits in length, and twenty cubits in breadth, and twenty cubits in the height thereof: and he overlaid it with pure gold; and so covered the altar which was of cedar. So Solomon overlaid the house within with pure gold: and he made a partition by the chains of gold before the oracle; and he overlaid it with gold. And the whole house he overlaid with gold, until he had finished all the house: also the whole altar that was by the oracle he overlaid with gold.

schools.summary: Delitzsch suspects the text has slipped, walls of the ceiling being very striking and probably a copyist's error for beams of the ceiling, and insists that the whole inside was covered with wood so nothing of the stone wall was seen. On the name of the inner room he reports the derivation as contested, Aquila and Symmachus rendering it a place of responses and the Latin oraculum, all from the verb to speak, which Hengstenberg adopts while most recent commentators follow a different lead. He agrees with Kimchi that the word rendered in the forepart is the construct of a noun meaning the interior, worries the derivation of the adjective for fine gold, and calls the words about the chains very obscure, withdrawing his earlier view that the house meant the party wall and taking the verb in the Chaldee sense of bolting. Ellicott prefers the marginal reading of the lining, holds the sense of in the forepart to be clearly in the inner part on the authority of the Latin and of Gesenius, judges the chain-work most probably a golden chain across the entrance before the veil, corrects our translators for anticipating the gilding when the altar was covered with cedar, and explains that the altar of incense, though standing before the veil and so in the holy place, was reckoned to belong in idea to the holy of holies.

Gill keeps the plain English of in the forepart and builds an architectural conclusion on it: the forepart is what stood before a man's face as he entered, and since the twenty cubits of height leave ten unaccounted for, the back part must have risen to the full thirty while the forepart was lower and open, to let in the light of the candlesticks and the smoke of the incense. He also takes the oracle as a speaking-place without hesitation, and alone puts a figure on the gilding, six hundred talents, or something over three million pounds sterling.

Clarke is brief through this stretch, referring back to his earlier notes on the roofing and forward to the description he prints at the end of the chapter, and saying of the gold only that it is impossible to calculate the expense or the quantity employed in the building.

Henry attends to material and ornament, cedar being strong, durable and of a very sweet smell and the wainscot carved with knops like eggs or apples and with flowers, no doubt as the fashion then was. He takes the oracle for the speaking-place, so called because thence God spoke to Moses and perhaps to the high priest when he consulted the breastplate of judgment, and observes that Solomon made everything new and more magnificent than it had been except the ark, which was still the one Moses made. On the gilding he notes that it was not washed over like ours but laid on the whole house, and turns the fact round: gold was under foot there, as it should be in all the living temples, the abundance of it lessening its worth.

debates.question: What does in the forepart mean?

positions.position: In the inner part, as the Latin renders it and as Gesenius explains the word
The interior, the form being the construct of a noun so meaning
Literally the front, so that the back part rose higher and the forepart was left lower and open

debates.question: Is the derivation of the name of the inner room settled?

positions.position: Yes, the oracle or speaking-place, thence God spoke to Moses
No, the derivation is doubtful, though the ancient versions and Hengstenberg take it from the verb to speak

debates.question: What were the chains of gold before the oracle?

Either a chain-work decoration on the partition or, more probably, a golden chain across the entrance before the veil as a guard against intrusion

outliers.claim: Holds that our translators were misled by the context into anticipating the gilding, the meaning being that Solomon covered the altar, presumably of stone, with cedar rather than with gold

23.pericope_label: And within the oracle he made two cherubims of olive tree, each ten cubits high. And five cubits was the one wing of the cherub, and five cubits the other wing of the cherub: from the uttermost part of the one wing unto the uttermost part of the other were ten cubits. And the other cherub was ten cubits: both the cherubims were of one measure and one size. The height of the one cherub was ten cubits, and so was it of the other cherub. And he set the cherubims within the inner house: and they stretched forth the wings of the cherubims, so that the wing of the one touched the one wall, and the wing of the other cherub touched the other wall; and their wings touched one another in the midst of the house. And he overlaid the cherubims with gold.

schools.summary: Ellicott gives the fullest treatment of the cherubim in the chapter. He notes that they are described in only three places in the Old Testament besides the visions of Ezekiel, which determined the imagery of the Apocalypse, and that in no case is their form distinctly mentioned, though a winged bull may perhaps be inferred by comparing two passages in Ezekiel, whence the golden calves of the later idolatry would naturally derive; against this he sets Josephus, who says no one can tell or even conjecture their shape, and concludes that the tradition must have been lost in the second temple, where there was no ark. Whatever they were, they were in no sense representations or emblems of Deity, like the winged figures of Assyria or Egypt with which they have often been compared, but appear rather to symbolise the great physical forces of the universe, guided by superhuman angelic intelligence to serve the supreme will of God. From the span of the wings he concludes that these figures faced the entrance where the tabernacle pair faced the mercy seat. Delitzsch takes the wood for oleaster or wild olive, very firm and durable, and gives the figures a human form like the golden cherubs on the ark, standing upright on their feet.

Gill observes that the phrase is oil tree and that pine and cypress yield oil too, which some think are meant, though the Targum says olive, and he lists the differences from the pair Moses made: larger, of olive wood rather than gold, and standing on the floor instead of rising at the two ends of the mercy seat and made out of it. He allows that they may be emblems of the angels in their greatness and glory, always in God's presence, but prefers to read them of the two witnesses who are called the two olive trees standing before the God of the whole earth, and carries the reading into the gilding, which may denote the purity and excellency of angels or the gifts and graces adorning the witnesses.
Clarke contributes the height in modern measure, about eighteen feet and three inches, and refers the question of their form to his note in Exodus rather than settling it here.

Henry explains why figures of this size were needed at all, the most holy place being much larger than in the tabernacle, so that the ark would have seemed lost in it and the dead wall unsightly unadorned; he says they were images of young men, as some think, of olive wood overlaid with gold. On their meaning he sets them against the heathen practice: the heathen set up images of their gods and worshipped them, but these represent the servants and attendants of the God of Israel, the holy angels, and were not to be themselves worshipped, only to show how great he is whom we are to worship.

debates.question: What form did the cherubim have?

Images of young men, as some think
Nowhere distinctly stated; possibly a winged bull by inference from Ezekiel, though Josephus denies that anyone can even conjecture
The great physical forces of the universe guided by angelic intelligence, and in no sense emblems of Deity
The servants and attendants of the God of Israel, the holy angels, set up not to be worshipped but to show how great he is
The angels, or rather the two witnesses called the two olive trees standing before the God of the whole earth

29.pericope_label: And he carved all the walls of the house round about with carved figures of cherubims and palm trees and open flowers, within and without. And the floor of the house he overlaid with gold, within and without. And for the entering of the oracle he made doors of olive tree: the lintel and side posts were a fifth part of the wall. The two doors also were of olive tree; and he carved upon them carvings of cherubims and palm trees and open flowers, and overlaid them with gold, and spread gold upon the cherubims, and upon the palm trees. So also made he for the door of the temple posts of olive tree, a fourth part of the wall. And the two doors were of fir tree: the two leaves of the one door were folding, and the two leaves of the other door were folding. And he carved thereon cherubims and palm trees and open flowers: and covered them with gold fitted upon the carved work. And he built the inner court with three rows of hewed stone, and a row of cedar beams.

schools.summary: Delitzsch explains the gilding method, gold leaf spread so that, as Rashi observes, every elevation and depression of the carving was impressed on the coating and plainly seen, and notes that ancient gilding was generally done by laying on gold plate fastened with tacks; he rejects Thenius's inference that the gilding was therefore confined to the engraved figures. On the doors he fights hardest: the words about the posts being a fifth are obscure and have been read in very different ways, but can hardly mean anything but that the projecting framework occupied a fifth of the wall's breadth, the alternative of posts of a fifth thickness having no support in Ezekiel and requiring both an unwarranted sense for one word and a wall two cubits thick. He explains the change of wood, cypress for the holy place rather than olive as lighter and so less likely to sink, and reads the cedar beams of the court as possibly set upright for a palisading so the people could see through. Ellicott asks how far the carving went, notes the minute accuracy with which the gold is said to be spread on one set of doors and fitted on the other, turns the proportions into dimensions, and prefers to read the court as an enclosing wall rather than a planked floor, since the altar and the laver stood there.

Gill reads the ornament rather than measuring it: if the cherubim stand for angels, the palm trees fitly represent just and upright men, who appear in the church below and in heaven above, where the open flowers of divine grace are also seen. He takes the doors of the oracle as typical of Christ, the door into the church above and below and the true olive tree, and identifies the inner court as the court of the priests, so called to distinguish it from the outer court where the people assembled.

Clarke takes the three rows of hewn stone and the row of cedar beams as alternating courses running all through the wall and asks whether such a building could be durable. He observes that the palace was built the same way, so this was probably the ordinary manner for better buildings, notes that Calmet refers to this mode the stone crying out of the wall and the beam answering it in the prophet, and adds that here at least the timber was not exposed to the weather, as it was not in the outer court.

Henry reads the proportions of the doors and the low wall of the court for what they teach. The folding doors into the oracle were a fifth part of the wall and those into the temple a fourth, both beautified with cherubim engraven on them. The inner court, where the brazen altar stood and the priests ministered, was separated from the people's court by a low wall of three rows of hewn stone tipped with a cornice of cedar, and he gives the reason: that over it the people might see what was done and hear what the priests said to them, for even under that dispensation they were not kept wholly in the dark or at a distance.

37.pericope_label: In the fourth year was the foundation of the house of the Lord laid, in the month Zif: And in the eleventh year, in the month Bul, which is the eighth month, was the house finished throughout all the parts thereof, and according to all the fashion of it. So was he seven years in building it.

schools.summary: Ellicott glosses the month-names, Zif as the brightness of flowers, about May, and Bul as the month of rain, about November, making seven years and a half in all. Delitzsch derives Bul differently, from a word for produce, so that it is the fruit month, and supposes the name came from the Phoenicians, with whom fruit ripened later, adding that it is said to be found on the great Sidonian inscription. He also judges the pace of the work: compared with other large buildings of antiquity and of modern times it was done in a very short time, and he cites Pliny on the two centuries all Asia spent at the temple of Diana at Ephesus.

Clarke finds it rather strange that the house needed seven years and six months, since the stones and timbers were prepared before they came to Jerusalem, and resolves it by the ornamenting, gilding and carved work; he notes that the round seven of the text is properly seven and a half, Scripture generally expressing things in round numbers. He reaches independently for the same comparison as Delitzsch, the temple of Diana, and questions whether Solomon's house cost anything like it. His best observation follows: the temple was never intended to hold a vast concourse of people, the courts and chambers being far more extensive than the temple itself, so it was never designed as a place to worship in but a place to worship at. Declining to describe the building himself, he prints an account borrowed from Calmet, whose argument is that Kings and Chronicles describe the temple properly so called but scarcely the courts and open areas, which Ezekiel supplied; one discrepancy is left standing, Ezekiel making the side chambers four cubits wide where this chapter allows five, six and seven.

Henry judges the work quickly done, considering the vastness and elegance of the building and all its appurtenances: Solomon was in earnest, had money enough, had nothing to divert him, and many hands made quick work. He then sets out what the house was a type of, in four stages: Christ the true temple, who spoke of the temple of his body; every believer a living temple built on Christ; the gospel church the mystical temple, where only Jews built the tabernacle but Gentiles joined in building the temple, and the door into the house was wider than the door into the oracle, many entering into profession who come short of salvation; and heaven the everlasting temple, its streets pure gold in allusion to this flooring, and there, as here, no noise of axes.

debates.question: Was seven years and a half a long time or a short one?

positions.position: Rather strange that it took so long, the stones being ready beforehand, and to be explained by the ornamenting and gilding
A very short time by comparison with other large buildings of antiquity and of modern times
Soon done, Solomon being in earnest, having money enough and nothing to divert him

debates.question: What does the month-name Bul mean?

positions.position: The month of rain
The fruit month, from a word for produce, the name probably Phoenician

outliers.claim: Observes that the temple was never designed to be a place to worship in but a place to worship at, the priests alone being employed within while the tribes came before God in the courts outside
